To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

implicit theories of intelligence are less incremental when considering individuals with Down syndrome than considering typical people, and the stronger the entity theory of intelligence, the more negative the judgments expressed explicitly, and the stronger implicit attitudes toward people.

the belief that intelligence is malleable is stronger when considering typical people rather than people with intellectual disabilities and that the belief that it is fixed predicts more negative judgments about people with intellectual disabilities.

implicit theories of intelligence concerning people with Down syndrome are less incremental than implicit theories of intelligence of typical people, and that this is related to more negative explicit judgments and more negative implicit attitudes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an understanding of the social representations of intelligence in people with intellectual disabilities and their impact on the social cognition of professionals and lay people.
the implicit theories of intelligence held by people with Down syndrome and the consequences of these beliefs on judgments of their intelligence.
the development of an implicit theory of intelligence in people with Down syndrome and the consequences of these beliefs in terms of explicit judgments and implicit attitudes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of this study are of interest to all those who work with people with Down syndrome and other intellectual disabilities, and that they are of interest to the general public, who may be interested in learning about the importance of beliefs about intelligence.

implicit theories of intelligence of individuals with down syndrome were less malleable than those of typical people, which was associated with negative explicit judgments of the intelligence of these people.

implicit theories of intelligence, and particularly the entity theory, have an important influence on the judgments made about the intelligence of people with Down syndrome and that these judgments are more negative than those about typical individuals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more you believe that intelligence is fixed, the more you believe in the intellectual disability of a person with Down syndrome, and the more negative your attitude toward that person.
people with Down syndrome are seen as more fixed than typical individuals, and the more fixed they are perceived, the more negative judgments are expressed.

implicit theories of intelligence are a powerful factor that influences the way people think about individuals with intellectual disabilities, and that this is a factor we should be aware of when working in the field.
The main takeaway from our work is that
implicit theories of intelligence of individuals with disabilities are less incremental than for individuals without disabilities.
people working with people with intellectual disabilities may be more likely to adopt a fixed view of intelligence when considering the latter.

implicit theories of intelligence of individuals with disabilities, and especially people with Down syndrome, should be considered as key elements to be taken into account when designing interventions for these people.
